title: Khaybar
hook: A fortress town, a flag for a man with sore eyes, and a meal that was poisoned.

screens.text: **At Khaybar, someone tried to kill him.** A poisoned meal was set in front of him. He had the power to punish. Watch what he chose.
**Why Khaybar?** In 7 AH he marched on Khaybar, a fortified town north of Madinah. Its leaders, IslamQA reports, had been rallying tribes against the Muslims [IslamQA 11575].
bubbles: As in every battle episode, we tell the history, not the fighting. His rule held here too: no harming women or children [Bukhari 3015].

screens.prompt: He said he'd give the flag to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger, and is loved by them. Everyone hoped it was them. Who got it?

options.text: 'Ali, who was at home with sore eyes
options.feedback: Right. He sent for 'Ali, prayed over his eyes, and they healed. Then he handed him the flag [Bukhari 4210].

options.text: The strongest fighter in the army
options.feedback: Not quite. He described the man by love, not strength. It was 'Ali, whose sore eyes he healed [Bukhari 4210].
Not quite. Everyone hoped. He asked for 'Ali, who wasn't even there, and healed his eyes [Bukhari 4210].

screens.text: **Invite them first.** As 'Ali set out, the Prophet ﷺ told him not to rush, and to call the people to Islam first. If Allah guided even one person through you, he said, it would be better than the finest red camels [Bukhari 4210].

events.title: Khaybar
events.text: He marches on the fortress town to the north [IslamQA 11575].

events.title: A poisoned meal
events.text: Someone tries to kill him. He refuses revenge [Bukhari 2617].

events.title: Ja'far comes home
events.text: The emigrants return from Abyssinia, the early biographers report [Dar al-Ifta 175].

events.title: Next: Mu'tah
events.text: An army goes north, and three commanders are named.

screens.text: **A poisoned meal.** At Khaybar a woman served him meat she had poisoned, and he ate from it. His Companions asked whether she should be killed. He said no [Bukhari 2617].
bubbles: He felt the poison's effects for the rest of his life, until his final illness [Bukhari 4428].

cards.back: She tried to kill him. He would not have her killed [Bukhari 2617].
A chief's daughter, she became his wife after he freed her. She is honoured as a Mother of the Believers [Bukhari 4201; Q 33:6].
After years away, his cousin came home around this time. He embraced him with joy, the early biographers report [Dar al-Ifta 175].

screens.text: **No revenge for himself.** You met this in Day 73: he never took revenge for his own sake [Bukhari 3560]. At Khaybar it was his own life on the line, and he still held back. If someone hurts you for being Muslim, you don't owe them payback.

screens.situation: Tyler's roommate thought it'd be funny to slip bacon into Tyler's lunch without telling him. Tyler found out after eating half of it. He's angry and embarrassed.

options.text: Tell him calmly that it hurt and isn't okay, set a clear boundary, and leave it there
options.feedback: Yes. Speaking up protects him; skipping revenge keeps his character. That's the Khaybar way.

options.text: Get him back with a worse prank
options.feedback: Not quite. The Prophet ﷺ didn't take revenge even for poison. Payback rarely ends anything.

options.text: Say nothing and start eating alone in his room
options.feedback: Not quite. Holding back revenge doesn't mean hiding. He can speak up and protect himself.

chips: Why did the Muslims go to Khaybar?
Someone hurt me for being Muslim. What now?

steps: Think of a small hurt someone caused you recently
Choose not to pay it back today, in words or in actions
Ask Allah to soften your heart, and theirs

screens.text: Someone tried to kill him, and he refused revenge. Strength isn't paying people back. It's being able to and choosing not to.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- In 7 AH he marched on Khaybar, a fortified town north of Madinah whose leaders, according to IslamQA, had been harming the Muslims and rallying tribes against Madinah [IslamQA 11575] (single source; say "is reported").
- He said he would give the flag to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger and is loved by them; he sent for 'Ali, who had eye trouble, prayed over him and his eyes healed; he told 'Ali to proceed without haste, invite them to Islam first, and said that one person guided through him is better than red camels (the most prized possessions of the time) [Bukhari 4210].
- A woman served him poisoned meat; asked whether she should be killed, he said no [Bukhari 2617]. In his final illness he said he still felt the pain of the food he ate at Khaybar [Bukhari 4428].
- Safiyyah bint Huyayy, daughter of a chief, was taken captive; he freed her and married her, and her freedom was her mahr [Bukhari 4201]. His wives are honoured as Mothers of the Believers [Q 33:6]. (scholar question Q40, Q41)
- Ja'far and the emigrants returned from Abyssinia after Khaybar; Dar al-Ifta reports he embraced Ja'far, unsure whether he was happier at Khaybar or at Ja'far's return [Dar al-Ifta Egypt, seerah part 9] (single organisation; "the early biographers report").
- His rules of war applied: no killing of women or children [Bukhari 3015]. (scholar question Q39)

**Likely questions**
- *"Why did the Muslims attack Khaybar?"* Keep to the history: a fortified town whose leaders are reported to have been organising tribes against Madinah [IslamQA 11575]. It was a political and military conflict, not a war on a religion. Don't describe the fighting. No rulings about fighting today (Day 71 frame). (scholar question Q39)
- *"Wasn't Khaybar Jewish? Does Islam hate Jews?"* No. Day 73 shows him standing for a Jewish man's funeral. The Qur'an honours the earlier prophets and calls Jews and Christians People of the Book. Khaybar was a conflict with a town's leaders, not a verdict on a people. Never connect it to Jews today, and no polemics.
- *"Who was Safiyyah? Was she forced to marry him?"* Say plainly: she was taken captive after the battle; slavery and captivity existed everywhere at that time; he freed her and married her, with her freedom as her mahr [Bukhari 4201]; she is honoured as a Mother of the Believers. Don't speculate about her feelings beyond the sources. Detailed questions about captives, or about his marriages, go to the imam. (scholar question Q40, Q41)
- *"Why did he marry so many times?"* Give the one calm line from seerah-40 (monogamous with Khadijah for about 25 years; later marriages mostly to widows or divorcees, many tied to alliances and care) and offer the imam. (scholar question Q41)
- *"Someone hurt me for being Muslim."* Listen first. No revenge doesn't mean no boundaries: speak up calmly, protect yourself, and involve the mentor. If there's danger, follow the safety rule.

**Escalate:** detailed questions on captives and slavery (Q40) or on his marriages (Q41); any question about fighting today (Day 71 frame and the imam); any unsafe situation (safety rule).

**Don't**
- Don't describe the fighting or give casualty numbers.
- Don't name the poisoner's religion on a screen or use the story against any group.
- Don't romanticise or debate Safiyyah's marriage; give the facts and offer the imam.
